title: Lesson 9. Responsive design, media queries
description: meta viewport, @media, breakpoints, mobile-first and desktop-first

learn.intro: Hi! Lesson 9 — **responsive design**. One site is opened both on a phone (375px) and on a big monitor (1920px). We'll learn to adapt a page to any screen. Let's go!

slides.text: If sizes are fixed in px (for example `width: 1000px`), on a phone the site spills off the screen: a horizontal scroll appears and cards get cut. To see a site on a phone without a phone: **F12 → the phone icon (Ctrl + Shift + M)** → choose iPhone or iPad.

`width=device-width` — the site width equals the screen width. `initial-scale=1` — no zoom in or out. Without this line a phone thinks it is a computer: it draws the site about 980px wide and just shrinks it, so the text gets tiny. **Without it, media queries don't work on a real phone.** Tip: in VS Code type `!` and press Tab — the line is already in the template.

check.prompt: What happens without meta viewport on a phone?
options: The site is drawn ~980px wide and shrunk, the text gets tiny
check.explain: The phone thinks it is a computer.

check.prompt: Without meta viewport media queries don't work on a real phone.
check.explain: This line is needed in every HTML.

slides.text: A media query is a condition in CSS: if the screen width is 768px or less, apply these styles instead of the usual ones.

`max-width: 768px` — «up to 768px, including 768px». Inside `@media` we write ordinary CSS, but **only what changes**. Important: write the media query **below** the ordinary styles — CSS reads top to bottom, a lower rule replaces an upper one.
Breakpoints (remember): up to **600px** — phone, up to **1024px** — tablet, over 1024px — computer.

check.explain: max means «at most», for small screens.

check.prompt: Match the width and the device

slides.text: **Desktop-first**: base styles for desktop, the `max-width` condition («up to…») — for small screens we remove extras. **Mobile-first**: base styles for phones, the `min-width` condition («from…») — for large screens we add.

Companies often use mobile-first: most people visit from a phone. For beginners `max-width` is easier — we already know desktop layout and now adapt to small screens. To remember: `max` is «at most», i.e. small screens; `min` is «at least», i.e. large screens.

check.prompt: Which condition does mobile-first usually use?
In desktop-first the base styles are written for desktop.
check.explain: And for small screens extras are removed.

sections.title: Examples: a menu and a gallery

slides.text: A menu: in a row on desktop, in a column on a phone. Only **one property** changes, no need to repeat `display: flex` and `gap`:
A gallery: 3 → 2 → 1 columns. Only the number in `repeat` changes:
**Order matters:** 1024px first, then 600px. If you swap them, the 1024px rule wins on a phone and 2 columns remain, because 375px is also below 1024px.

options: Otherwise the 1024px rule wins on a phone
check.explain: 375px is also below 1024px, so the lower rule must be 600px.
